clips.title: Claude Code — For Teams & Enterprise
clips.why: A short tour of server-managed settings: one settings file that an organisation pushes to every Claude Code, instead of each person editing their own.
look: What server-managed settings are: one settings file an admin writes in the claude.ai admin console, which every Claude Code in the organisation receives.
Ask yourself why this beats a page of setup instructions: nobody has to type anything, and one change reaches everyone.
Think of our telemetry block as one more part of this file: the same eight variables, the same for everyone.
clips.after: Our telemetry settings travel this way, and the ingest token lives only in that admin console, never in the copy of the file we keep in git.

clips.title: Track AI Token Usage by Team & Feature in Claude Code with OpenTelemetry (Part 4)
clips.why: He labels Claude Code's numbers by team and feature with OpenTelemetry resource attributes, which each developer sets on their own machine.
look: The OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES line: a list of name=value pairs that is attached to every number the process sends.
Watch who sets the team name in his setup, and ask yourself what happens when someone moves to another team.
Ask yourself what the team numbers look like when one developer forgets, or types the wrong team.
clips.after: We keep his idea but move the team out of people's hands: our settings carry only department=rnd and source=human, and the collector turns each email into a team from one table.

clips.title: OTTL in Action: Stop Shipping Junk Telemetry to Your Backend
clips.why: The collector's transform language, OTTL, used for exactly our job: find personal data such as an email and replace it with a SHA-256 hash.
look: Each statement is a function with an optional where condition, the same shape as our set(...) where attributes["user.email"] == ... lines.
The SHA256 converter: the same input always gives the same hash, so you can still count different users without knowing who they are.
Ask yourself about the order: the email has to be hashed before it is removed, or there is nothing left to hash.
clips.after: Our collector runs the same kind of statements: one set() per person for the team, then a salted SHA256 for the hash, then delete_key for the email.

practice.q: A laptop sends cost numbers to otel.rhinohealth.com without an Authorization header. Where is the request stopped?

options.text: At the WAF, because it only lets company laptops through
options.why: The WAF looks for attack patterns, not for who is calling. The address is public on purpose, so laptops off the VPN can reach it.

options.text: In the collector's receiver, by bearertokenauth, before any processor runs
options.why: The receiver hands every request to the extension first. No token means 401, and nothing reaches the pipeline.

options.text: In VictoriaMetrics, which refuses points without a token
options.why: VictoriaMetrics never sees the request. The collector stops it long before an exporter could send anything.

practice.q: Finish the managed settings line so every Claude Code sends the token in the standard header.
practice.hint: The same header name you use when you call an API with a Bearer token.
practice.why: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS is a list of name=value pairs. The exporter turns this one into the header Authorization: Bearer <token> on every request.

practice.q: Your collector configuration defines bearertokenauth and uses it in the receiver's auth block. You deploy, and the collector does not start: "authenticator not found". What is missing?

options.why: An extension is only started when service.extensions lists it. The receiver asks for an authenticator that never started, so the collector refuses to run.
A missing token gives a different error: "no bearer token provided". Both stop the collector, which is the safe way to fail.

options.text: A processor that checks the token
options.why: Processors never check tokens. The receiver checks the token through the extension, before any processor runs.

practice.q: Put the statements of the people step in the order the collector must run them for one data point.
items: set the team from the email, one statement per person in the table
set the team to "other" when no statement matched
set user.hash to the SHA-256 of the email plus the salt
practice.why: Every step needs the email except the last one. Delete it first and there is nothing left to look up or hash, so the email must be the last thing to go.

practice.q: An agent's VM must also send its numbers. Which design fits the rule that a VM holds no long-lived secret?

options.text: Bake the ingest token into the VM image, because it can only write
options.why: Write-only is fine for a laptop, but a VM reads text that anyone can write, and anything on it can be sent away. The rule has no exceptions for small secrets.

options.text: Send to a small relay in the LLM gateway with the run token; the relay adds the ingest token
options.why: The run token is short-lived and only valid for this run. The ingest token stays on the server side.

options.text: Turn telemetry off on agent VMs and read the cost from the Anthropic invoice
options.why: The invoice has no agent, ticket or step, so you could never say which run or which step spent the money.
